canberra.title: ‘All about equity’: 18 schools big losers in 2027 budgets but government refuses to name them
canberra.snippet: Eighteen public schools will lose more than 5 per cent in funding for 2027, compared with this year’s allocation, but the ACT Gover...
canberra.content:
There are winners and losers in the ACT public school funding shake-up, but the government won’t say who they are. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

Eighteen public schools will lose more than 5 per cent in funding for 2027, compared with this year’s allocation, but the ACT Government won’t name them.

All schools received their final projected budget and staffing profile for the 2027 school year on Tuesday (17 November), but these will be reviewed when final enrolments are known in February.

Principals were advised at noon today, and parents also received a general letter about the budget allocation, but without any specifics about their school’s situation.

Twenty-two schools will enjoy a budget increase of more than 5 per cent, but the bulk of schools, 52, go either way with a budget variance of between -5 per cent and +5 per cent (inclusive).

The government has listed the budget breakdown – including core funding, the equity allocation and the exceptions funding – for all schools online but without any comparison with previous funding.

When challenged by journalists that this was not the transparency the government had promised, Education Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith referred them to the MySchool website. However, she said a direct comparison would not be accurate.

Ms Stephen-Smith said the government did not want a league table of school funding published, saying schools and their principals needed to be protected.

“What we have seen over this period has been an identified psychosocial risk for individual school principals being identified, with those schools being identified as having particular challenges around staffing or around budgets, and individual school principals having to go back to their communities to correct misinformation that has been provided to and through the media,” she said.

“What we don’t want is to see individual school principals being identified, being approached by the media, to get their responses.

“Now those principals know if their school has been previously overallocated that they are going to have to make some decisions to fit within the resourcing allocation that is fair and equitable across our public education system.

“But those principals do not deserve to be targeted in relation to either media commentary or commentary from their school communities.”

Education Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith says the budget outcome was about equity.

The government secrecy overshadowed the announcement, which Ms Stephen-Smith said would mean a fairer distribution of funding across all ACT schools, as recommended by the School Resourcing review.

“This is fundamentally about a fairer distribution of the funding that we have in the system today and ensuring that there is equity between our schools,” she said.

Ms Stephen-Smith said ACT public schools would continue to receive the highest funding per student in the nation, with the ACT being the only jurisdiction that funds above the National School Resourcing Standard.

The government has budgeted $1.2 billion for the public school system in 2026-27, up 7.3 per cent from the previous year, including an additional $40.58 million to support schools’ transition to the new funding model.

$25.5 million has been allocated for the 2027 school year to support the introduction of the Adjustments-Based Resourcing Model for students with disability, and specialist schools will receive $11.2 million above their Student Resource Allocation funding in 2027, increasing their funding above 2026 budget levels.

An additional $7 million will be provided across the system to support Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students, on top of the existing Cultural Integrity Allocation.

Ms Stephen-Smith said 13 schools, named online, would receive specific exceptions funding to help them manage the transition.

She said no specialist school would lose out in the funding shake-up, and would receive more than in 2026.

Other supports for schools include additional funding for students with disability whose needs are beyond what can be supported in the school, the allocation of allied health and social workers, and subject matter experts to assist in timetabling to manage resources more efficiently.

Australian Education Union ACT president Angela Burroughs says government needs to grow the pie.

Ms Stephen-Smith would not say if some learning support assistants would lose their jobs, but the Directorate, as part of the shift to a single system, was looking at a more mobile workforce, both permanent and casual, to deploy where needed across schools.

She said some schools had in the past been over-resourced, at the expense of other schools.

By region, Tuggeranong schools would end up receiving additional funding compared to previous years. Gungahlin was the only region where schools would see a slight reduction in funding.

Ms Stephen-Smith said schools may have to cut extracurricular activities, timetable differently or combine classes to cope with a tighter budget.

She recognised that losing funding would be challenging and disappointing for some school communities, but appealed to them to understand this was about equity across the system.

“So if you’re in a school where funding has previously been over-allocated, and you’ve had a lot of extracurricular activities compared to another school, think about the fact that other public schools in the system are now going to be getting a bit of a fairer go,” she said.

Australian Education Union ACT president Angela Burroughs said the government needed to increase the budget, not just take money from some schools to give to others.

Ms Burroughs said the government at least now knew that 48 schools, or more than half of the ACT’s public schools, were experiencing significant resourcing pressure, and that was something it could not ignore.

“Are our schools all at the moment able to offer a full five-day-a-week timetable? Are they able to operate without constantly splitting and collapsing classes?” she said.

“If they can’t, there’s not enough resources in the system because there is no school that is overstaffed.

“So that requires injection of resources. That doesn’t necessarily have to be money. It could be infrastructure, it could be centralised support, but what they haven’t done is provide that at the moment.”

Ms Burroughs said it was also concerning that the government had whittled down the 43 schools identified as under extreme resourcing pressure to just 13 through the Directorate’s own self-assessment over the weekend, without one single conversation with someone who worked in those schools.

She said multiple members had told her that they were preparing for a horror 2027, having to cope with fewer staff.

Ms Burroughs said the government should come clean on what schools would lose and gain.

canberra.title: Gotta steal ’em all: Burglar nabs Pokémon cards worth thousands
canberra.snippet: A serial burglar has been sentenced for a string of crimes, including stealing thousands of dollars’ worth of Pokémon trading cards...
canberra.content:
17 November 2026

These Pokémon cards were recovered after being stolen in a burglary in February 2026. Photos: ACT Policing.

A serial burglar has been sentenced for a string of crimes, including stealing thousands of dollars’ worth of Pokémon trading cards from a Canberra store.

Jack Carbone rode an e-bike to the Collector’s Colosseum store in Acton in the early hours of 6 February 2026 and forced his way inside, the ACT Supreme Court’s Justice Verity McWilliam said in her recently published decision.

He ripped four display cases off the wall, which contained high-value Pokémon cards, and took a plastic display case from the counter containing unopened packs of the popular cards.

Carbone forced the cases open and tried to steal all of their contents before riding away.

When police arrested and searched him the following month, they found he still had three of the high-value Pokémon cards. One was worth $2000 and another was worth $550.

Police then searched a home linked to Carbone in Belconnen, where they seized two phones and a tin containing assorted Pokémon cards.

“The motivation was obviously personal gain,” Justice McWilliam said.

“The items stolen were of high value. Although there was a dispute about their precise value, I accept that the stolen cards were worth many thousands of dollars, and because they were expressly collectors’ items, they were difficult/impossible to replace.

“Many of the cards were not recovered.”

This was actually the last burglary Carbone committed.

Justice McWilliam said in August 2024, he and another man broke into the Beer Wine Spirits store in Kambah and stole nearly $11,000-worth of cigarettes and nearly $2000-worth of alcohol.

The following day, he was one of three men who used a sledgehammer to break into Liquorland Chisholm, where they stole 176 packets of cigarettes and cash.

About an hour later, the trio broke into the SPAR supermarket in Rivett, where they unsuccessfully tried to open a cigarette unit and safe.

Carbone pleaded guilty to one count of burglary and three counts of burglary by joint commission and spent 255 days in custody before he was sentenced earlier this week.

The father-of-one is now aged in his mid-30s. Justice McWilliam said he had a severe substance use disorder at the time of offending, which contributed to the burglaries.

He wrote letters to the court in which he told the victims of his crimes that he felt remorse and wished he could undo the damage he caused.

Justice McWilliam took into account the time he had already spent in custody when saying she would sentence him to a Drug and Alcohol Treatment Order, which is a rehabilitation-focused and community-based sentence.

“Plainly, removing the criminogenic risk factors of drug and alcohol addiction must be given priority. It is through rehabilitation that the long-term protection of the community will be promoted,” she said.

Carbone was sentenced to four years and two months’ jail, with the remainder suspended for him to complete a three-and-a-half-year Drug and Alcohol Treatment Order.

This means he was allowed to leave custody to complete a residential rehabilitation program.

canberra.title: Labor’s expected backdown on backpacker visa changes confirmed
canberra.snippet: It’s official: Labor has backed down on parts of its get-tough plan for backpacker visas amid constant pressure from the hospitality and ...
canberra.content:
Immigration Minister Tony Burke consulted with industry and regional communities after announcing the migration policy. Now he’s had to change that policy. Photo: Facebook.

It’s official: Labor has backed down on parts of its get-tough plan for backpacker visas amid constant pressure from the hospitality and agriculture lobbies – not to mention from the Brits.

Immigration Minister Tony Burke has let everyone in on the Federal Government’s worst-kept secret, announcing on Tuesday (17 November) that the planned visa changes were being tweaked again.

The proposed cap on third-year visas under the flagged new ballot system will rise from 5000 to 25,000. That’s a huge difference, and closer to the 31,000 in that group last year.

But the number of days Working Holiday Maker (WHM) visa holders must serve in the regions to be eligible for a second year will increase from 88 to 120.

That’s an increase from three to four months.

“This creates a very significant shift, but also means that for the people who are wanting to qualify for their second year, we’re getting more regional days out of them,” Mr Bourke said from Cairns.

Those on current WHM visas will have until 28 February 2027 to complete the relevant specified work and lodge a valid application under the existing process.

From 1 March 2027, people seeking a second or third WHM visa (except UK citizens) will need to hold a Next Year Regional Work Guarantee.

People will receive the guarantee by registering their interest and being invited to apply. A portal to register interest will be open from 1 December 2026.

There will be 45,000 second visa places and 25,000 third visa places in 2026–27.

While the specified work requirement for a second visa will increase from three months to four months from 1 March 2027, work completed before that date will count towards the new requirement. The requirement for a third visa will remain at six months.

After registrations open in December, the first monthly invitation round is expected in mid-January 2027.

Registrations will remain valid until 30 June 2027. An invitation will be valid for 12 months and will allow a person to apply for a visa.

The Opposition has described the new announcement as a “shambolic backdown” on backpacker visas.

Nationals leader Matt Canavan said the latest version of Labor’s migration policy proves Labor did not listen to regional industries or the business sector before Mr Burke made his initial announcement at the National Press Club in September.

“The government’s migration policy, announced just months ago, has not even made it through to Christmas,” Senator Canavan said.

“The Coalition and industry stakeholders warned very clearly that Labor’s original proposed restrictions would threaten regional jobs, businesses and agricultural production.

“These are industries that depend on Working Holiday Makers to fill genuine workforce shortages, especially in regional communities where finding enough local workers is already a serious challenge.

“Instead of consulting with and listening to those industries before making its original announcement, Labor pressed ahead with poorly conceived restrictions and created completely unnecessary uncertainty for regional employers and Working Holiday Makers.”

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said the whole thing was “complete nonsense” and committed a future Coalition government to repealing any ballot system.

“They’ve created a complete mess with this raffle, this ballot,” he said.

“They’ve said they’re going to delay it … they should just axe it.”

But Mr Burke said the government had been “working constructively” with peak industry groups on the design of the new system since the day after his Press Club address (but apparently not before then).

“Working Holiday Makers make an important contribution to our economy, especially in agriculture, tourism and hospitality and in regional Australia,” he said on Tuesday.

“But when demand grows too fast, the government needs the tools to manage the program properly. The registration process is a fair way to do that.

“These changes give businesses and Working Holiday Makers clear rules and time to plan, while making sure the program continues to support the regions and industries that rely on it.

“Australia will continue to welcome Working Holiday Makers. These reforms make the program fairer, more targeted and sustainable for the long term.”

The minister wouldn’t shed any further light on “discussions” with the UK Government over Australia’s plans to change current arrangements for British backpackers.

Right now, under the free trade agreement between the two nations, British backpackers are not required to work in regional areas.

Australia wants to change that, but the UK Government is applying the brakes.

Mr Burke described the current arrangements as “not a good outcome” for Australia and said talks were going “very well” on why it should be changed to some degree.

“We’ve got constructive conversations that are continuing with the United Kingdom, and I’m optimistic that we’re going to get a much better deal than was previously negotiated,” he said

“The United Kingdom has a good understanding of the issues that we need to resolve.

“So I’m not going to put a timeline on it, but I will say I’m very optimistic about how those conversations have been going.”

canberra.title: Woman accused of grooming, abusing underage boy named
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse. A woman accused of plying an underage boy with alcohol and grooming him for ...
canberra.content:
17 November 2026

Heather Mariah Brady, 22, entered not guilty pleas to her four charges in the ACT Magistrates Court. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse.

A woman accused of plying an underage boy with alcohol and grooming him for a sexual relationship has announced she will fight all of her charges.

According to the allegations in court documents, 22-year-old Heather Mariah Brady was working as a youth care worker for an organisation in Canberra when she met the boy, who was under 16, through mutual connections.

She allegedly groomed and indecently abused him earlier in 2026 before she was arrested and granted bail that October.

Ms Brady faced the ACT Magistrates Court again on Tuesday (17 November), where her lawyer, Julia McLean of Hugo Law Group, said she would enter pleas of not guilty to all four charges.

Magistrate Alexandra Burt then adjourned the matter to 26 January 2027.

Ms Brady, who is from the ACT suburb of Page and remains on bail, was charged with grooming, committing an act of indecency on a person under 16, supplying liquor to a young person and using a carriage service to procure sexual activity with a person under 16.

She was fired from her job in July 2026 when her employer heard allegations that she had been providing vapes and alcohol to children.

While Region did not name her in its original reporting due to last-minute concerns by police, no legal attempt to suppress her name has been made in court since then.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to police by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

Right now, the centre of global diplomacy has shifted to our region as world leaders descend on Asia for back-to-back summits in the Philippines and China.

Anthony Albanese is currently in Manila for the Asean summit, where he is due to meet with Donald Trump along with other leaders.

Then later this week the city of Shenzhen will host an unprecedented three-way meeting between Trump, the Chinese president, Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.

Nour Haydar speaks to Guardian Australia’s political editor Tom McIlroy, who is travelling with the prime minister.

australia.title: Paul Kelly pleads for Albanese to ‘show some backbone’ over AI as creatives campaign for copyright protections
australia.snippet: Music legend is joined by Jimmy Barnes and Peter Garrett in backing Not AI’s To Take campaign ahead of Aria awards Get our breaking news ...
australia.content:
Australia’s creative community has launched a major campaign pleading with the Albanese government not to water down copyright law amid furious lobbying from AI companies, ahead of Wednesday night’s Aria awards.

Music legends Jimmy Barnes, Paul Kelly and Peter Garrett are among those backing the Not AI’s To Take campaign, supported by dozens of creative groups representing the recording, writing, publishing, film, television and media industries.

While the government maintains it will not undermine copyright law, the industry minister, Tim Ayres, said on Tuesday “the status quo is no good” for the creative sector, ahead of a package of AI legislation expected by early 2027.

But creatives have pushed back on such claims, arguing copyright law doesn’t need updating – just better enforcement, and that changes could put the $70bn creative industry and its 600,000 workers at risk.

“[AI platforms] haven’t made one phone call yet. They haven’t called us. They haven’t called anybody,” said Dean Ormston, CEO of music rights organisation Apra Amcos.

“There’s nothing wrong with the copyright framework. The problem is getting somebody to sit at the table and have a discussion with us.”

Not AI’s To Take is backed by the likes of Aria, the Copyright Agency, the Australian Directors’ Guild, Screen Producers Australia, the Australian Society of Authors, the Australian Writers’ Guild, and media organisations including Foxtel, Free TV, Nine, Seven and Guardian Australia.

Australian musicians including Montaigne and KLP have backed the campaign online, while Guardian Australia understands Barnes, Kelly and Garrett – some of Anthony Albanese’s favourite musicians – will also feature.

“Our government has been a huge supporter of Australian music and creativity, and now we’re asking them to continue that support by standing firm on copyright and making sure big tech doesn’t get to rewrite the rules at the expense of creators,” said KLP, real name Kristy Lee Peters.

In quotes shared on the campaign’s website, Barnes said: “I think that these companies should go and f..k themselves.”

Kelly is quoted as saying: “Australia has had some of the best copyright laws, something to be proud of. Now is the time for our government to show some backbone.”

Although Albanese has declared it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, some AI companies have argued it is too difficult to make individual licensing deals under existing copyright law. AI companies have said they need legal certainty on the copyright issue before investing and training models in Australia, with Anthropic putting forward an “opt-out” model to scrape creative works unless a rightsholder objected.

However Anthropic told a Senate committee it would “provide ongoing access to frontier models to eligible Australian entities, regardless of whether training is permitted.”

The government is expected to unveil a long-awaited legislative package on AI in late 2026 or early 2027, with proposals around datacentres, online safety, productivity and copyright. Albanese said last week that artists “need to be compensated if their work is used”. But the creative community is concerned that lobbying from big tech may sway government decisions.

“This isn’t a smear campaign. We’re just making some noise out in the open, where tech companies are doing it in the shadows,” said Patrizia Di Biase-Dyson, CEO of the Australian Publishers Association.

“Everything is at stake. We have to do as much as possible to educate everyone.”

Ormston said creative industries welcomed the investment and opportunities of AI, and had applauded both Labor’s rebuffing of a text and data mining exemption and Albanese’s public support. But he said artists were worried about potential changes.

“Our very clear message to the government has been: hold firm. You are absolutely saying the right thing. You are absolutely right in the fact that while we want AI in this country, we want it on Australia’s terms,” Ormston said.

Asked about the campaign on Tuesday, Ayres said “nothing has changed in terms of the government’s approach” to copyright.

“I understand the anxiety, though. For those workers, the status quo is no good for them. Their work is currently being appropriated, today, offshore. We have set out a program for a scheme of legislation that would protect those rights, make sure that artificial intelligence investment in Australia is on Australia’s terms.

“We’re not about undermining copyright here. That commitment has been made so many times now.”

A spokesperson for the attorney general, Michelle Rowland, said the government was “committed to supporting” creatives, and pledged any copyright changes would “deliver meaningful control and fair compensation”.

But independent senator David Pocock urged caution around any moves, warning that copyright changes could create a legal “loophole” to make Australia a global “data laundering hotspot”.

“There are more than 100 court cases on foot involving copyright and AI training in the US and we should wait for these to play out before making any changes given the risks of getting it wrong are so high,” he said.

australia.title: ‘We don’t want our city to lose its storytellers’: Sydney artists awarded $25k in Australian first – no strings attached
australia.snippet: City of Sydney’s inaugural ‘living grants’ program aimed at retaining city’s ‘creative soul’ Get our breaking news email , free app or da...
australia.content:
Julian Hamman feels like a “great weight” has been lifted from his shoulders. Yesterday the 26-year-old film-maker from Sydney was calculating how many more casual shifts he would need to pick up as a gallery host and paramedic assistant in order to finance his creative work.

But last night, Hamman found out he is one of 40 creatives to receive an “artist living grant”, a new initiative from the City of Sydney which awards him a catch-free lump sum of $25,000 to simply continue living and working as a creative.

“From my casual jobs I’ve made around $25,000 [this year] and a lot of that goes towards groceries and having to fit my schedule around my work,” he says. “The brain task-switching you do when you work freelance and two jobs is exhausting … Having a base income will allow me to focus on my practice and have some brain space.”

Totalling $1m, the 40 new grants were approved by the council on Monday night, awarding no-strings-attached direct payments not tied to specific projects, based on a successful basic income for artists introduced in Ireland three years ago. Ireland’s pilot scheme was made permanent in February 2026, giving 2,000 creative workers €325 a week.

“Our research shows artists are leaving Sydney due to low incomes, rising costs and limited resources,” Sydney’s lord mayor, Clover Moore, said in a statement. “We don’t want our city to lose its local storytellers and creative soul.

“While it’s not a cure all, these grants will boost 40 Sydney artists working across a range of artforms at different points in their careers, with many from under-represented communities.”

According to Creative Australia’s most recent report, practising professional artists in Australia earned average gross incomes of $54,500 in the 2021-2022 financial year, comprising $23,200 in creative income, $15,300 in arts-related income, and $16,000 in non-arts income.

The first of its kind in the country, Sydney’s $25,000 grant is open to artists of all disciplines, from all over the city – not only those who live in the City of Sydney catchment.

Kamilaroi and Tongan musician David Leha, who makes music as Radical Son, is another recipient. He applied for the grant in August, and says the money will help with living costs, touring costs and promoting his music.

“It won’t pay for one thing, but it will help with all things,” says the 50 year old, based in Liverpool. “I have been in the arts now for 25 years and it hasn’t been easy, especially in the last decade. There’s a saying that you often have to pay to play and in some cases we’re losing money to perform, so to be able to get this support is really helpful. The costs go on and on.”

Leha splits his time between writing, recording and touring new music and studying for a PhD in creative studies at the University of Newcastle. Along with the rising cost of living, he says the particular challenges he faces as a First Nations musician make it difficult to make enough money from music alone.

“We are expected to have a social media presence and unfortunately some venues are booking based on your following rather than the quality of the music itself, and as First Nations artists our stories are so diverse, but it might not necessarily translate to getting bums on seats.”

Morgan Hogg, a multidisciplinary artist of Cook Island Māori (Ngāti Tāne), Tahitian and English descent, is another recipient of the inaugural grant.

“It’s such a pivotal time in my career,” she says. “I’m about five years into my career as a professional artist and it’ll mean having more time to dedicate to my practice. I’m very grateful.”

The 26-year-old, based in Ashfield, supports her career with a casual job at the Sydney College of the Arts. “Some weeks I’ll work an eight-hour shift, and some days I’ll work 20 hours a week. It depends on how much work they have for me and how much time I need to spend on art projects.”

Hogg estimates she spends the majority of her time as an artist on admin, such as identifying and applying for arts grants. “For a project for next year alone I have applied for seven different grants, and I write them all myself … it probably takes me two to three weeks outside of my normal job and I don’t necessarily get paid for it. Probably 80% of my role as an artist is doing admin.”

The $25,000 grant, which is expected to be paid to all 40 artists by the end of the year, will help fund Hogg’s travel to the Cook Islands, Tahiti and Rapa Nui (Easter Island) for two video works, which involve working with traditional knowledge holders in the region.

The City of Sydney says it will not dictate how the grant money is spent. It can fund any aspect of creative practice, living expenses and the costs of producing new work.

“There are no specific requirements to ‘create’, or restrictions on other work, meaning the money can be spent on … whatever the artist needs,” said City of Sydney Greens councillor Sylvie Ellsmore in a statement. Ellsmore put forward a motion for an artist’s basic income three years ago, which led to this new grant.

“Sydney is losing more artists than any other capital city, because it’s so expensive to live here. Meanwhile too much arts funding is still being allocated to big name, commercial festivals, who often don’t pay artists enough – or at all,” she said.

“Basic income models are how we should be funding the arts – with money going directly to artists, musicians, writers and creators, no strings attached.”

australia.title: Chris Minns’ backflips are adding up. Is he ‘clearing the runway’ or panicking?
australia.snippet: From train timetables to coffee cups and property underquoting, the NSW premier is making policy reversals well ahead of the March electi...
australia.content:
If recent coverage is to be believed, the New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, is a talented gymnast. A last-minute intervention by the premier on Monday afternoon, the day before a suite of reforms on underquoting were due to take effect, marks a quadruple or quintuple policy “backflip” by Minns in recent weeks, depending on who you ask.

The laws banning real estate agents from lowering the advertised price of a property beneath a previously rejected written offer have been shelved for up to a year, after the premier flagged on Monday morning he had received concerns from estate agents in his own electorate about their effect amid a housing market downturn.

The NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, said the move was “government by 2GB”, referencing the Sydney talkback radio station which had also raised the issue on Monday morning.

“But this isn’t the first time” she told presenter Ben Fordham on Tuesday.

First, the government backed down last month from implementing changes to several local and regional rail line timetables after criticism from commuters.

Next, after a social media post by Sloane, it changed gender-neutral language of “carer” and “lactating parents” in a new parliamentary breastfeeding policy to reflect what Minns said was “commonsense language like ‘mother’ and ‘breastfeeding’”.

After the Daily Telegraph ran a “Nup to the Cup” campaign against plastics legislation, which included requiring cafes to offer dine-in customers mugs and glasses instead of takeaway cups, the government dropped the changes, which would not have been implemented until 2028.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

This weekend, it made an election promise of a two-year funding guarantee for community preschools after the opposition had warned the sector was facing a $150m annual cut from January.

But Eamonn Fitzpatrick, a lobbyist and former communications and campaign advisor to federal and state Labor governments, says the reversals are more about “clear air” than pre-campaign jitters as the government enters the final sitting days before the March election.

“That is the job of this final sitting week, let’s not forget you go into summer. It’s a dead period,” says Fitzpatrick, who worked alongside Minns in the office of former Labor premier Morris Iemma.

“What you’re seeking to do, actually, in either putting things on hold, changing your minds, revising policies, you’re actually just minimising distraction … clearing the runway.”

Fitzpatrick says interventions are part of Minns’ brand as a strong leader, but insists his style is no more top-down than previous premiers.

Minns has consistently polled ahead of Sloane as preferred premier but he has made no secret about the threat from One Nation, whom he and his ministers have started to refer to as the state’s unofficial opposition.

Peter Lewis, the non-executive chair of strategic communications company Essential, which undertook qualitative research for Labor in the last federal election, said recent polling suggested voting intention in November in NSW was at 27% for Labor, 26% for One Nation and 23% for the Coalition.

Lewis says he thinks the threat of One Nation in NSW is being “used to push the political debate towards the right and could be used as an excuse for the government not to embrace more progressive policies”.

“I wonder if there is a bit of a mistake in that. One Nation voters are being driven by dissatisfaction with the status quo and so governments that are seen as actually addressing issues probably have a better case to answer.”

Defending its underquoting backflip, Labor has said it is protecting buyers from being shut out of sales at lower prices amid a downturn which has seen home values in Sydney drop by 10.1% from their 2026 peak, according to data from Cotality.

In question time, the fair trading minister, Anoulack Chanthivong, whose department was responsible for the reforms and who has now been overruled for a third time by Minns on policy, said the market had changed and the government had responded.

Both he and Minns pointed out that Sloane and the opposition had supported the underquoting laws at the time, which were conceived for a “rising hot market”.

But, Lewis says “there is a cost in being seen to change a position” – and points to Peter Dutton’s 2025 federal election campaign as an example.

“Maybe Minns has done this early enough in the cycle for it not to be an issue, but as you get close to the election it changes, particularly when they’re walking back commitments that have been made to benefit people.

“It can be read as panic.”

world.title: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
world.snippet: Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’ Five EU member ...
world.content:
Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.

The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.

In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.

Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.

In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.

Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania, it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.

The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.

The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe.

Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said it was “a huge breakthrough”.

The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”

Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”

Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government, which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.

Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, said on Monday the move had no “future or humanity”. “I don’t see any future or humanity in that. It’s not the solution,” Sanchez, an outspoken defender of immigration in a Europe that has tilted to the right in recent years, told Telecinco television.

The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She said: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union, with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”

Alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, said it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.

“On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.

Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.

Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.

world.title: US basketball player arrested with 75lb of marijuana at Nigerian airport, say authorities
world.snippet: Suspect named as Greene Da’monte Khiree Drug smuggling carries life sentence in Nigeria An American basketball player has been arrested i...
world.content:
An American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly attempting to smuggle 33.95kg (75lb) of marijuana into the country.

Nigeria’s National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said a 28-year-old player named as Greene Da’monte Khiree from the state of Georgia was arrested at Lagos’s main airport last Wednesday after he arrived on a flight from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.

The NDLEA said the player told them he had come to Nigeria to “build networks” for his basketball career. The agency said evidence on his phone suggested he had “knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity”. The NDLEA said it detained the player when he attempted to leave the airport with his hand luggage after abandoning two checked-in bags. The agency said those two bags were found to contain 32 parcels of marijuana, and a tracking device.

Nigeria has strict drug laws, and trafficking carries a sentence of life in prison.

A basketball player by the name of Damonte Greene is listed on the roster of the Pattani Raptors in the Thai Premier Men’s League. Greene, a Georgia native, played college basketball for Reinhardt University and South Georgia Technical College. He played semi-professional basketball in the US before representing a number of teams in Thailand.

WNBA star Brittney Griner and former Utah State player Jarred Shaw were imprisoned in Russia and Indonesia respectively for marijuana offenses. Griner was released in December 2022, while Shaw remains in prison.

world.title: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests
world.snippet: Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human The ...
world.content:
The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.

The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.

The growth in both baboon and human populations in Cape Town in recent years has led to increased conflict and more baboons dying as a result. Meanwhile, a heated debate has raged between people who believe that baboons and humans can coexist and those who argue that baboons in urban areas are in danger and in some cases need to be relocated. Some animal rights activists have compared authorities’ baboon management to apartheid.

During Friday’s relocation, outraged protesters tried to stop vehicles taking the baboons away. One person sprayed a fire extinguisher, according to the Daily Maverick, a local news outlet.

After the confrontation, the local Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals branch urged those opposed to the baboons’ capture not to try to stop the vehicles. “Capture and transport are already stressful for the baboons,” it said in a statement. “Delaying their arrival prolongs their time in crates and risks adding to that stress – this is not fair on the baboons.”

It said it remained opposed to the baboon’s relocation, adding: “Our presence did not imply support … our inspectors are present because the animals need someone looking out for them.”

On Sunday, dozens of people sat outside the wildlife centre in a silent protest, some tying flowers to the fence. Baboons from a different troop also gathered at the boundary, calling to the newly captive animals, the Daily Maverick reported.

“We stand together for the Seaforth and Waterfall troops, for their freedom, their dignity and their right to live as wild animals,” Mandy Neal, the administrator of the Save Kogelfontein Baboons Facebook group, posted on Monday, calling for weekly Sunday silent protests. “ Our message is simple: CAPTIVITY IS NOT CONSERVATION.”

The City of Cape Town said in a statement on Sunday that the relocation had been successful, with the baboons being monitored 24/7 after being checked by vets and the females receiving contraceptive implants.

It said: “The Waterfall troop has been relocated due to the severity and persistence of human-baboon conflict in the Simon’s Town urban environment, the limited available natural low-lying habitat, the increasing risk to the baboons’ welfare, and public safety concerns … [and] as a very last resort after other interventions were evaluated and deemed ineffective, and as an alternative to culling.”

Prof Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town, said the baboon management plan had undergone two years of public consultations. “It has thus been disappointing watching members of the public and select NGOs, many which did not engage in the stakeholder process, now compromising the safety and welfare of the baboons and people through violent actions directed at staff and baboons in transit.”

world.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
world.snippet: After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-...
world.content:
The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.

Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.

Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.

The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement: “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”

She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.

“Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”

Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.

Vara’s article prompted outrage online, with many claiming that Black writers, and Africans in particular, were being unfairly singled out by allegations of the use of AI.

Associated Press contributed to this report

world.title: Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah crossing and Gaza aid facilities
world.snippet: Seven-time F1 world champion tours border area and logistics warehouses operated by Egyptian Red Crescent Lewis Hamilton has visited Egyp...
world.content:
Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.

The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.

“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October.

A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.

Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.

Airstrikes also continue, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.

Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid to Gaza.

At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.

Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.

The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.

The first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.
